lessons.title: Usage of A
lessons.description: Learn when to use A before singular countable nouns.

sections.heading: 1. Basic Rule
sections.content: Use A before a singular countable noun that begins with a consonant sound.

examples.explanation: Book begins with the consonant sound /b/.
Teacher begins with the consonant sound /t/.

sections.heading: 2. Introducing Something
sections.content: Use A when mentioning one non-specific person or thing for the first time.

examples.explanation: The man is being introduced for the first time.
A problem is mentioned without identifying a particular problem.

sections.heading: 3. Professions
sections.content: Use A before a singular profession or occupation when describing what someone is.

examples.explanation: Doctor is a singular profession beginning with a consonant sound.

examples.sentence: She works as a software engineer.
examples.explanation: The phrase begins with the consonant sound /s/.

sections.heading: 4. Rate and Frequency
sections.content: A can mean 'per' or 'each' in expressions of rate, speed and frequency.

examples.sentence: The car travels at 60 kilometres a hour.
examples.explanation: This sentence is incorrect. The correct expression is '60 kilometres an hour' because hour begins with a vowel sound.
A means each or per in this expression.

sections.heading: 5. Important Conditions
sections.content: A is generally used with singular countable nouns. It is not normally used directly before plural nouns or uncountable nouns.

examples.explanation: Chair is a singular countable noun.
The plural noun chairs does not take A.
Water is uncountable in this general meaning.

lessons.title: Usage of An
lessons.description: Understand how An is used before words beginning with vowel sounds.

sections.heading: 1. Basic Rule
sections.content: Use An before a singular countable noun that begins with a vowel sound.

examples.explanation: Apple begins with a vowel sound.
Orange begins with a vowel sound.

sections.heading: 2. Vowel Sounds
sections.content: The important factor is pronunciation. Words beginning with A, E, I, O or U often take An when their first sound is a vowel sound.

examples.explanation: Egg begins with a vowel sound.
Insect begins with a vowel sound.
Octopus begins with a vowel sound.

sections.heading: 3. Silent Initial Letters
sections.content: Some words begin with a written consonant that is not pronounced. Use An if the first pronounced sound is a vowel.

examples.explanation: The H is silent.
The H is silent.
The H is silent.

sections.heading: 4. Abbreviations
sections.content: Use An before an abbreviation when its spoken first letter begins with a vowel sound.

examples.explanation: M is pronounced 'em'.
F is pronounced 'ef'.
X is pronounced 'ex'.

sections.heading: 5. Avoiding Common Errors
sections.content: Do not choose An just because a word starts with a vowel letter. Check its first sound.

examples.explanation: University begins with the consonant /y/ sound.
European begins with the consonant /y/ sound.

lessons.title: A vs An
lessons.description: Practise choosing between A and An based on the first pronounced sound.

sections.heading: 1. The Main Difference
sections.content: A is used before consonant sounds. An is used before vowel sounds. Both are indefinite articles used with singular countable nouns.

examples.explanation: Car begins with /k/, a consonant sound.
Umbrella begins with a vowel sound.

sections.heading: 2. Same Letter, Different Sound
sections.content: A word's spelling does not always tell you which article to use. Pronunciation is what matters.

examples.explanation: The initial U is pronounced with a /y/ sound.
The initial U has a vowel sound.

sections.heading: 3. Numbers and Letters
sections.content: Choose the article according to how the number or letter is pronounced.

examples.explanation: Eight begins with a vowel sound.
One begins with the consonant /w/ sound.

sections.heading: 4. Abbreviations
sections.content: For letter-by-letter abbreviations, listen to the first letter's spoken name.

examples.explanation: M is pronounced 'em'.
U is pronounced 'you'.

sections.heading: 5. Quick Revision
sections.content: Remember: A for consonant sounds and An for vowel sounds. Never decide only by looking at the first letter.

examples.explanation: House has a pronounced H; hour has a silent H.
European begins with /y/; engineer begins with a vowel sound.

lessons.title: Articles with Silent H
lessons.description: Learn how silent H changes the choice between A and An.

sections.heading: 1. What Is Silent H?
sections.content: In some English words, the letter H is written but not pronounced. When the first pronounced sound is a vowel, use An.

examples.explanation: The H in hour is silent.
The H in honest is silent.

sections.heading: 2. Common Silent H Words
sections.content: Some commonly used words with silent initial H include hour, honest, honour and heir.

examples.explanation: The H is silent in honour.
The H is silent in heir.

sections.heading: 3. Pronounced H
sections.content: When H is pronounced as a consonant sound, use A.

examples.explanation: The H is pronounced.
The H is pronounced in standard modern usage.
History begins with a pronounced H.

sections.heading: 4. Context and Pronunciation
sections.content: Article choice follows the pronunciation used by the speaker. Some H words have had variation in pronunciation across accents and historical usage.

examples.explanation: In standard modern pronunciation, the H in historic is pronounced.
Hour begins with a vowel sound.

lessons.title: Articles with U and EU Sounds
lessons.description: Understand why some words beginning with U or EU take A instead of An.

sections.heading: 1. The /y/ Sound
sections.content: Words beginning with a U or EU spelling may start with the consonant /y/ sound, as in 'yes'. Use A before these words.

examples.explanation: University begins with /y/.
European begins with /y/.

sections.heading: 2. More Examples
sections.content: Several common words beginning with U or EU have this initial consonant sound.

examples.explanation: Uniform begins with /y/.
Unique begins with /y/.
Usual begins with /y/.

sections.heading: 3. U Words with Vowel Sounds
sections.content: Some words beginning with U start with a vowel sound instead. Use An before them.

examples.explanation: Umbrella begins with a vowel sound.
Uncle begins with a vowel sound.
Unusual begins with a vowel sound.

sections.heading: 4. Compare the Sounds
sections.content: The same written letter can represent different initial sounds. Always listen to the word.

examples.explanation: University begins with /y/; umbrella begins with a vowel sound.
European begins with /y/; urgent begins with a vowel sound.

lessons.title: Articles with Abbreviations
lessons.description: Learn to select A or An before abbreviations and initialisms.

sections.heading: 1. Letter-by-Letter Pronunciation
sections.content: When an abbreviation is spoken as separate letter names, choose A or An according to the first spoken letter's sound.

examples.explanation: M is pronounced 'em', beginning with a vowel sound.
F is pronounced 'ef', beginning with a vowel sound.

sections.heading: 2. More Examples
sections.content: Some letter names begin with vowel sounds, while others begin with consonant sounds.

examples.explanation: N is pronounced 'en'.
L is pronounced 'el'.
B is pronounced 'bee', beginning with a consonant sound.

sections.heading: 3. Abbreviations Pronounced as Words
sections.content: When an abbreviation is pronounced as a word, choose the article based on the first sound of that spoken word.

examples.explanation: NASA is pronounced as a word beginning with /n/.
UNESCO is pronounced as a word beginning with /y/.

sections.heading: 4. Common Mistakes
sections.content: Do not select an article by the first written letter alone. Say the abbreviation aloud and identify its first sound.

examples.explanation: U is spoken as 'you', which begins with /y/.
X is spoken as 'ex', which begins with a vowel sound.

lessons.title: First Mention of a Noun
lessons.description: Learn how A and An introduce a person or thing for the first time.

sections.heading: 1. Introducing a New Noun
sections.content: Use A or An when introducing a singular countable noun that is not yet known to the listener.

examples.explanation: The woman is introduced for the first time.
The coin is introduced for the first time, and old begins with a vowel sound.

sections.heading: 2. Referring to It Again
sections.content: After introducing a noun with A or An, use The when referring to that same identifiable noun again.

examples.sentence: I saw a bird. The bird was colourful.
examples.explanation: The bird is now identifiable because it was introduced earlier.

examples.sentence: She bought an umbrella. The umbrella is blue.
examples.explanation: The second sentence refers to the same umbrella.

sections.heading: 3. First Mention Does Not Always Mean A or An
sections.content: A noun may take The on its first mention when the context already makes it identifiable to the listener.

examples.explanation: The door is identifiable from the shared physical situation.
The context may identify which principal is meant.

sections.heading: 4. A and An Are Not Used with Every Noun
sections.content: A and An are used with singular countable nouns, not directly with plural or uncountable nouns in their general meanings.

examples.sentence: I saw birds in the garden.
examples.explanation: Birds is plural, so A or An cannot be used.
Information is uncountable, so it does not take A or An directly.

lessons.title: Common Exceptions and Mistakes
lessons.description: Review tricky pronunciation patterns and frequent errors involving A and An.

sections.heading: 1. Spelling vs Sound
sections.content: The first sound, not the first letter, determines whether A or An is used.

examples.explanation: University starts with /y/, a consonant sound.
Umbrella starts with a vowel sound.

sections.heading: 2. Silent Letters
sections.content: Some written letters are not pronounced. Select the article according to the first sound you actually hear.

examples.explanation: The H is silent.
The H is silent.

sections.heading: 3. Words Beginning with One
sections.content: Words beginning with one often start with a /w/ consonant sound, so they take A.

examples.explanation: One begins with /w/.
One begins with /w/.

sections.heading: 4. Avoid Articles with Plural and Uncountable Nouns
sections.content: Do not use A or An directly before plural nouns or uncountable nouns when they are used generally.

examples.explanation: Advice is uncountable. Say 'a piece of advice' when referring to one item.
Children is plural and does not take A or An.

sections.heading: 5. Correcting Common Errors
sections.content: Check the noun type and its first pronounced sound before choosing an article.

examples.sentence: Incorrect: an useful book. Correct: a useful book.
examples.explanation: Useful begins with the consonant /y/ sound.

examples.sentence: Incorrect: a hour. Correct: an hour.
examples.explanation: Hour begins with a vowel sound because H is silent.
